pr_body:
Fixes https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/104995

The default implementation for `nullable()` for binary operators return `false` if both the operands are not null.
This is used to prune IS NOT NULL conditions from the queries.

For ESQL it's not valid, eg. we can still return null in case of:
- multi-values: `[1, 2] + 3` --> null
- overflows/calculation errors: `1 / 0` --> null


A practical example:

```
ROW a = 5, b = [ 1, 2 ] 
    | EVAL sum = a + b
    | LIMIT 1
    | WHERE sum IS NOT NULL
```

For this query, the optimizations replace `sum IS NOT NULL` with `true`, assuming that `a+b` is always not null just because both `a` and `b` are not null.


This PR covers binary conditions (`==`, `>`, `>=`...), regex operators (`LIKE/RLIKE`) and math operators (`+`, `-`, `*`...).

We'll need a follow-up PR for functions, because the same criterion is applied also in that case, and it's even more likely to fail, because of exceptions in function execution.
pr_title: ES|QL: Fix nullability checks on binary operators
pr_comment: Hi @luigidellaquila, I've created a changelog YAML for you.

(sorry, long post)

@astefan @bpintea thanks for your feedback. 

First of all, let me try to clarify the problem here, probably my initial explanation did not go in depth enough.

In QL, nullability is a concept with its own semantics, independent from foldability. The planner treats the two aspects separately. The nullability checks don't do folding (they can't do it, most of the times child expressions won't even be foldable), but only rely on the nullability of child expressions.
To be precise and complete, the dependency is inverse: folding optimization rules use nullability, so if there is a bug in the nullability logic, there is a potential bug also in folding.

The vast majority of binary conditions, operators, functions, rely on the base class implementation, ie. [Function.nullable()](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/x-pack/plugin/ql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/ql/expression/function/Function.java#L47), that uses [Expressions.nullable()](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/x-pack/plugin/ql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/ql/expression/Expressions.java#L83). I'll report the code here for clarity

```java
    public static Nullability nullable(List<? extends Expression> exps) {
        Nullability value = Nullability.FALSE;
        for (Expression exp : exps) {
            switch (exp.nullable()) {
                case UNKNOWN:
                    return Nullability.UNKNOWN;
                case TRUE:
                    value = Nullability.TRUE;
                    break;
                default:
                    // not nullable
                    break;
            }
        }
        return value;
    }
```

The logic is simple: if all the arguments are not nullable, then the expression is not nullable.
If at least one of the arguments is nullable/unknown, then the expression is nullable/unknown.

I think we can agree that `Nullability.FALSE` is a strong statement: if an expression declares to be non-nullable and then returns `null`, it's a bug.
On the other hand, `Nullability.TRUE` doesn't make any assumptions: an expression can safely return `null` or a non-null value according to its business logic, and both would be reasonable in terms of nullability.
`Nullability.UNKNOWN` is someway blurry, in this case the expression can still return `null` or a non-null value, and it would still be reasonable (exact same as Nullability.TRUE). The only reason I find for the existence of this option is to delay the decision. 
(UNKNOWN does not seem to be an option for us, it is used in a tricky way by SQL and its applicability to ESQL is not clear; using it instead of TRUE makes things even worse in terms of test failures)

The logic described above doesn't fit into ESQL logic.

In ESQL an expression (a comparison, a math expression, a function) can be null even if all its arguments are not nullable:
- it applies to multi-values: `[1, 2] + 3` --> `null`
- it applies to single values
  - for NaN: `1 / 0` --> `null`
  - for overflows: `1.7976931348623157E+308 + 1.7976931348623157E+308` --> `null`

In short, that logic is good for SQL probably, but not for ESQL.

In ESQL, the only reliable way to know if an expression returns NULL is to fold it, but folding relies on nullability, so I cannot create a loop dependency here (more a conceptual loop rather than a stack overflow, the nullability is used in folding optimization rules, not in `fold()` methods fortunately). And in general, the spirit of nullability in QL seems to be to speculate on expressions without the need for folding.

[edit]
Actually, this is not about folding at all, the same problem can also happen with non-foldable expressions, see https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/105023#discussion_r1483132017
[/edit]

Andrei, to your objections:

> the aspect that doesn't fit is the inconsistency of single values being treated correctly (from nullability pov) while the multi-values not

As I said in the main comment, also single values are treated incorrectly; number overflows, division by zero, checked exceptions (for functions) can result in returning null, also for single values.

And in general, if we apply some logic, I think it has to be correct in all cases.

> And the inconsistency comes from the fact that FoldNull is already receiving a value folded to null for single-values, while for multi-values it does not, the multi-values do not come folded.

FoldNull [uses nullable()](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/x-pack/plugin/ql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/ql/optimizer/OptimizerRules.java#L1682), so it will wrongly fold expressions like `WHERE a + b IS NOT NULL` _because of this bug_.

> As an experiment (and I encourage you to explore other facets of this issue), take PropagateEvalFoldables from LogicalPlanOptimizer and place it right before FoldNull. Test your queries added as part of the PR and then test the entire suite.

I'll be honest, I disagree with this approach: even if the tests pass, the logical bug will still be there, just hidden behind some additional complications. 
The root cause of the problem seems clear to me, ignoring it does not seem logical.

Anyway, that rule swapping doesn't make a real difference, the problem is still reproducible with `ROW a = 5, b = [ 1, 2 ] | eval x = a + b |  WHERE a + b IS NOT NULL`

Thanks for your feedback @costin 
I'll open a new PR trying this approach. 

Just consider that the problem is not limited to `FoldNull`, there are at least two more rules that use `nullable()`:
- [PropagateNullable](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/x-pack/plugin/ql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/ql/optimizer/OptimizerRules.java#L1705) uses `nullable()` and will need a review as well
- [BinaryComparisonSimplification](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/x-pack/plugin/ql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/ql/optimizer/OptimizerRules.java#L268) practically depends only on `nullable()`, apart from NullEquals that we don't use in ESQL. This rule will have to be disabled completely

review_comment: Is this right? For something like `| eval x = 1, y = 2 | eval z = x + y | where z is not null`, the nullability of the addition should still be `FALSE`, right?

I don't think so. You'll know that the result is not null only after you fold it, but nullability does not rely on folding.

A practical example is `1.7976931348623157E+308 + 1.7976931348623157E+308`: both operands are not null, but the result is null (infinity)

> You'll know that the result is not null only after you fold it, but nullability does not rely on folding.

That of `Literal`s implicitly does, right? `Literal#nullable()` literally checks for `null`.
However, more generally, my intuition is that for expressions with literals only, when we can fold them, we should be able to establish the exact nullability, rather than be conservative (i.e. return the "worst": `Nullability.TRUE`). And this could manifest in the inter-play of the optimisation rules, not necessarily extend other `nullable()`s to check for values.

Otherwise, replacing `nullable()`s with `TRUE`s will make `FoldNull` effectively simply check if there's a `null` literal in the tree.

Also, when we'll get to broader MVs support, comparisons and other boolean predicates (comparisons, `LIKE`, `startsWith()` etc.)  can keep their children-delegating logic.

(However, your proposed solution is probably still a better intermediary step than current state.)

> we should be able to establish the exact nullability

I don't think nullability and folding to null should be mixed. If an expression is foldable, we have optimization rules that will do it for us and everything will work just fine, we just have to avoid messing up with nullability.

And consider that all this applies also to non-foldable expressions:

```
FROM idx | WHERE coalesce(a, 10) + coalesce(b, 20) IS NOT NULL
```

in this case you cannot even fold, because a and b are not foldable, but you can easily say that `coalesce(a, 10)` and `coalesce(b, 20)` are Nullable.FALSE (and still, `coalesce(a, 10) + coalesce(b, 20)` is Nullable.TRUE)

I think reasoning on folding is a red herring here.

> I don't think nullability and folding to null should be mixed.

Isn't that what `FoldNull` does: it folds ~to `null`~ based on nullability, tho just for `IsNotNull`/`IsNull`; and effectively, the proposed fix deactivates this check.

> I think reasoning on folding is a red herring here.

And the fix this PR proposes should extend to `coalesce()` too, besides the `EsqlArithmeticOperation`s, I think you're right.

However, the issue with comparisons &co. above stands. If the comparison would be folded before `FoldNull` gets to it, the change in this PR wouldn't be required anymore.
Edit: for non-foldable expressions, the `[Field]Attribute`s children would make the nullability `TRUE`, so not relevant.

Besides the MV issue: we don't do this now, but if we'd have `FieldAttribute`s' nullability set based on type and we'd compare two `constant_keyword`s, the `IsNull` _should_ be optimised away. With the proposed fix, this wouldn't happen anymore.
